title: Modify System Image: Downgrade System Image
shortTitle: Modify System Image: Downgrade System Image
summary: Downgrade System Image is the sub-technique of Modify System Image in which the adversary installs an older release of the device operating system instead of altering the current one. Older releases of network device firmware commonly ship weaker default ciphers, fewer hardening options, known and already fixed vulnerabilities, and less mature logging, so the adversary regains ground the vendor had closed. On embedded devices the swap usually means replacing the operating system file in storage, then reconfiguring the boot variable to load it, followed by a restart either immediately or at the next natural reboot. Because the device now genuinely runs vendor code, it may still pass a signature check on the image itself, so integrity verification alone is not enough. Detection therefore centres on version and inventory comparison: the reported version and build string against the approved release for that asset, image file names and sizes that do not match the standard build, boot variable changes, transfer logs for Trivial File Transfer Protocol or console sessions, and configuration files that suddenly contain settings only supported by older software. Peripheral evidence includes features or commands now missing, log formats changing, and a failure of settings that depend on newer firmware. Legitimate rollbacks happen after a bad upgrade and are recorded, short lived and tied to a known incident; malicious downgrades are unannounced, long lived and usually support further weakening such as reduced key length.

beginner.definition: Network devices run firmware, which is the operating system stored inside them. This sub-technique describes an attacker replacing today's version with an older one. The older version still works, but it protects the device far less well.
beginner.whyItMatters: New firmware usually fixes bugs and removes weak settings. Old firmware keeps those weaknesses, and some of them are publicly known. An attacker may also choose a version that makes encryption easier to break. Because the image is a genuine vendor file, a simple signature check may not notice anything wrong. You need to compare versions instead.
howItWorks: The attacker first gains administrative access to the target network device itself.
They obtain an older firmware file that matches the exact device model.
They transfer the older file to the device storage, often over an unencrypted protocol.
They change the boot setting so the device starts the older version.
They restart the device at once, or wait for the next planned restart.
The device then runs old software with weaker ciphers and missing fixes.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital night desk again, but this time the thief brings an old edition of the rulebook from five years ago. He swaps it for the current one on the desk. The book is genuine, printed by the same hospital, so nobody questions it. But this old edition never mentions the new medicine cabinet lock, and it allows entry to people the current rules exclude. The guard follows it faithfully and the desk looks normal. That is a downgrade. The device is running real vendor software, so it does not look fake, yet the rules have quietly rolled back to a time when the attacker had an easier path.
takeaways: Track approved firmware versions per device and alert on any unexpected change.
An unmodified older image can still pass a signature check, so compare versions.
Rollbacks should always follow an incident record and a plan to upgrade again.

objectives: Explain why older device firmware is less secure than current firmware.
Describe the steps used to replace an image with an older release and boot it.
Identify version, build and file artefacts that prove a downgrade occurred.
Explain why image signature checks alone may not detect this sub-technique.
Distinguish a planned rollback from a malicious downgrade.
Describe how a downgrade can support later encryption weakening.
